query: Eutectic high-entropy alloys contain dual-phase lamellar colonies with numerous internal boundaries, where microcracking can initiate and lead to catastrophic damage during room-temperature tensile deformation. Conventional processing commonly raises strength at the expense of ductility, while the wide range of previously proposed microstructural-design and processing strategies has not eliminated room-temperature brittleness and limited tensile ductility. Under these constraints, what single intervention could improve both strength and room-temperature tensile ductility? State one testable hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts outcomes relative to the unmodified lamellar-colony baseline, defines its boundary conditions, cites supporting prior evidence, and proposes an experiment whose result would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: A short-duration sub-solvus annealing treatment (~0.9× the eutectic melting temperature for 10–30 minutes), followed by a rapid quench, will simultaneously improve both room-temperature tensile strength and ductility in eutectic high-entropy alloys by reducing microcrack initiation along the fine lamellar interfaces while generating a controlled population of fine, coherent precipitates.
generation.material_initial_state: As-cast eutectic high-entropy alloy with a fine dual-phase lamellar fcc/B2 microstructure that contains numerous internal colony boundaries prone to microcrack initiation.
generation.intervention: A thermal/thermomechanical treatment consisting of a short-duration sub-solvus annealing at approximately 0.9× the eutectic melting temperature for 10–30 minutes, followed by a rapid quench.
generation.conditions: Room-temperature tensile deformation conditions; the treatment temperature must remain below the eutectic melting point to avoid full coarsening or phase instability, and the time window should be controlled (10–30 minutes) to balance limited lamellar coarsening with controlled precipitation.
generation.structural_mediator: Partial coarsening of the lamellae, reduction in boundary connectivity, and the formation of moderate fractions of fine, coherent precipitates.
generation.mechanism: The sub-solvus annealing reduces local stress concentrations at the interconnected lamellar boundaries by partially coarsening them, thus minimizing microcrack initiation. At the same time, the controlled precipitation from the thermal treatment adds a strengthening phase without compromising the ductility, as the precipitates remain coherent and facilitate dislocation transmission.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the unmodified as-cast lamellar microstructure, the treated alloy is expected to show increased yield and ultimate tensile strength as well as improved tensile ductility due to delayed crack initiation and balanced microstructural reinforcement.
generation.baseline: The as-cast eutectic HEA exhibiting a fine lamellar fcc/B2 microstructure characterized by high ductility (~25% elongation) but modest yield strength, with inherent microcrack susceptibility at the colony boundaries.
generation.boundary: This approach is effective only when the thermal treatment is precisely controlled (sub-solvus temperature near 0.9× melting point and short dwell time). Deviations (e.g., higher temperatures or longer annealing times) could lead to excessive coarsening or formation of undesirable brittle phases, nullifying the ductility benefits.
generation.uncertainty: The exact quantitative balance of strength and ductility improvements and the optimal processing window remain to be fully determined; uncertainties also exist regarding how slight variations in composition or processing may influence the treatment's effectiveness.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of eutectic HEA samples: one set as-cast (baseline) and the other subjected to the proposed sub-solvus annealing treatment (0.9× eutectic melting temperature for 10–30 minutes followed by rapid quench). Perform microstructural characterization using SEM/TEM to assess lamellar spacing, precipitate distribution, and boundary connectivity. Conduct room-temperature tensile tests to measure yield strength, ultimate tensile strength, and elongation.
measurements: Microstructural features (lamellar spacing, precipitate size and distribution, boundary connectivity) via microscopy.
Mechanical properties including yield strength, ultimate tensile strength, and ductility (percentage elongation) via tensile testing.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the treated samples do not exhibit both a statistically significant increase in tensile strength and an improvement in ductility compared to the as-cast baseline, or if microcrack initiation still occurs at similar or higher rates due to unchanged or aggravated boundary characteristics, the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text:
High-entropy alloys (HEAs) can have either high strength or high ductility, and a simultaneous achievement of both still constitutes a tough challenge. The inferior castability and compositional segregation of HEAs are also obstacles for their technological applications. To tackle these problems, here we proposed a novel strategy to design HEAs using the eutectic alloy concept, i.e. to achieve a microstructure composed of alternating soft fcc and hard bcc phases. As a manifestation of this concept, an AlCoCrFeNi 2.1 (atomic portion) eutectic high-entropy alloy (EHEA) was designed. The as-cast EHEA possessed a fine lamellar fcc/B2 microstructure, and showed an unprecedented combination of high tensile ductility and high fracture strength at room temperature. The excellent mechanical properties could be kept up to 700°C. This new alloy design strategy can be readily adapted to large-scale industrial production of HEAs with simultaneous high fracture strength and high ductility.

The bulk AlCoCrFeNi 2.1 alloy exhibited an excellent castability with few casting defects, significantly differentiating with other bulk HEAs. The tensile test specimen was machined from the bulk alloy ingot and is shown in Fig. 1b . The cast microstructure of AlCoCrFeNi 2.1 is shown in Fig. 2a . Even in such a bulk cast ingot, a uniform and fine lamellar microstructure characteristic of eutectic alloys was achieved. The inter-lamellar spacing was about 2 μm. An enlarged microstructure given in Fig. 2c shows that dense nanoscale NiAl-rich precipitates (marked as B II ) occurred in the CoCrFe-rich region. decision.trend: In the sole paper addressing a dual-phase lamellar AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic HEA (PMC4145285), researchers demonstrated that the as-cast lamellar fcc/B2 microstructure provides good ductility (∼25% tensile elongation) but modest yield strength. Cold rolling increases strength (to ∼1265 MPa) but sharply reduces ductility, underscoring the persistent trade-off between strength and ductility. Despite various microstructural refinements and post-casting treatments to improve strength, a robust solution for sustaining high ductility at room temperature remains elusive, as microcrack initiation at internal colony boundaries still induces brittle fracture.
decision.unsolved: Present approaches—whether simple cold rolling or other conventional thermo-mechanical processing—have not resolved the recurring dilemma of microcracking along dense lamellar interfaces. Refinements improve strength but often degrade room-temperature ductility. A concise process pathway to disrupt or mitigate microcrack initiation at colony boundaries while retaining, or enhancing, strength is still lacking.
decision.lever: A short-duration sub-solvus annealing (below the eutectic melting temperature) that partially coarsens the lamellae and generates a moderate fraction of fine, coherent precipitates, for example at ∼0.9× the eutectic melting temperature for 10–30 minutes, followed by a rapid quench.
decision.why: This tailored thermal treatment reduces boundary connectivity and local stresses at the fine lamellar interfaces—curbing microcrack initiation—while simultaneously stimulating controlled precipitation that imparts additional strength. Prior work (PMC4145285) shows cold working followed by heat treatment can refashion the lamellar structure; here, a carefully chosen sub-solvus soak and rapid quench should achieve a balanced microstructure. Testing the resulting mechanical response relative to the baseline as-cast lamellar EHEA would reveal whether microcrack suppression and strength gain occur. Should cracks still initiate at abundant fine-scale boundaries without increased strength, that outcome would falsify the proposed mechanism.
